title: Phishing Emails
about: Spot the warning signs of a fake email before you click.

cards.prompt: An email pops up while you're busy.

steps.text: **"Congratulations! You've won a games console! Click here within 1 hour to claim your prize."** You never entered a competition. What do you do?

choices.text: Click quickly, before the hour is up
choices.consequence: The rush is the trick. The link leads to a page that asks for your details or payment.

choices.text: Reply to ask if it's real
choices.consequence: Replying tells the scammer your address works, so you'll get more scams.

choices.text: Use your mail app's Report button, then delete it
choices.consequence: No prize is lost, because there never was one. Reporting helps your mail app catch the next one.

cards.explanation: A prize you never entered, plus a deadline, is a classic scam. **Don't click, don't reply**: report it and delete it.
cards.hint: You never entered a competition. So why would someone give you a prize, and why only one hour to claim it?

cards.title: Something fishy
cards.body:
That was **phishing** (said "fishing"): a message pretending to be someone you trust, like your bank, school or a game. A prize you never entered, with a rush to claim it, is classic bait: **too good to be true**. Real prizes never cost money to claim either.

Tap through the next email to meet more warning signs.

cards.prompt: Your Bank's real emails come from **@yourbank.example**. **Tap each part** of this email to meet a warning sign.

parts.job: Fake sender: anyone can type any name. The address after the @ is what counts. yourbank-help.example isn't Your Bank.
Rushing you: "Closed in 24 hours!" Pressure stops you thinking.
"Dear Customer": real companies usually use your name. But scammers can find names too, so a name proves nothing.
Asks for secrets: real companies never ask for passwords, codes, card numbers or PINs by email.
Hidden link: it really goes to yourbank-verify.example. Hover over a link, or press and hold it, to see where it goes.

cards.explanation: Five warning signs: a **fake sender**, **rushing you**, **"Dear Customer"**, **asking for secrets** and a **hidden link**. Plus **too good to be true** from the prize email.

items.label: A link to a different site than it says
Your school's usual email about a trip

cards.explanation: Rushing, asking for secrets, prizes you pay for and links that go elsewhere are phishing signs. The **real** address sending you to the official app, or your school's usual email, is probably fine.
cards.hint: Check each against the signs: fake sender, rushing, "Dear Customer", secrets, hidden links, too good to be true.
cards.nudge: Check each one again: does it rush you, ask for secrets, hide a link or want money for a prize?

cards.prompt: Your Bank's emails come from **@yourbank.example**. Tap **every** warning sign here (the time and sign-off are fine).
cards.explanation: The sender isn't `@yourbank.example`, the subject **rushes you**, it says **"Dear Customer"**, it **asks for secrets** and the button goes to `yourbank-verify.example`.
cards.hint: Go back over the five signs you just met. Each one is on its own line.
cards.nudge: There are five. Look for each sign you just met, one at a time.

cards.prompt: An email arrives that seems personal.

steps.text: **"Hi Sam, your school account will be deleted today. Sign in here to keep it."** It uses your real name and school. What do you do?

choices.text: Sign in with the link. It knows your name, so it's real
choices.consequence: Scammers can find names and schools online. Using your name doesn't make it real.

choices.text: Skip the link: sign in the usual way, or ask your teacher
choices.consequence: Your account is fine, and your teacher reports the scam to the school.

steps.text: Your friend Alex got it too and **already typed in their password**. Alex feels silly. What should Alex do?

choices.text: Keep quiet and hope nobody uses it
choices.consequence: Hiding it gives the scammer time to get in. Fixing it fast matters more than feeling silly.

choices.text: Reply to the email and ask them to delete it
choices.consequence: That goes straight to the scammer, and shows them the address works.

choices.text: Change that password straight away and tell a trusted adult
choices.consequence: Now the stolen password is useless. Alex isn't in trouble: scams fool adults too.

cards.explanation: A name doesn't prove a message is real: go to the site **your usual way**. If a password slipped out, **change it straight away** and tell a trusted adult. It's never your fault.
cards.hint: Can a name prove an email is real? And what makes a stolen password useless?

cards.prompt: Your Bank's website is `yourbank.example`. Which email address is **really** Your Bank's?

options.nudge: `yourbank-alerts` is a different name from `yourbank`: that's a lookalike.
The part after the @ is what counts. `mail-alerts.example` isn't Your Bank.

cards.explanation: Only `@yourbank.example` is Your Bank. `yourbank-alerts.example` is a lookalike, and in the last one the part after the @ belongs to someone else.
cards.hint: Look only at the part after the @. Is it exactly `yourbank.example`?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Phishing** pretends to be someone you trust.
- Check the **address after the @**, not the name.
- Don't click: **go there yourself**, report it, tell an adult.

Next: scams in texts and phone calls.
